section_title: Money Laundering Risks in Financial Services > Control and ownership for AML compliance

propositions.proposition: When reviewing ownership structures, there is a regulatory obligation to identify the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) of the customer.
source_quotes: When reviewing ownership structures, there is a regulatory obligation to identify the UBO of a customer.

propositions.proposition: For AML purposes, to identify the UBO, one must aggregate direct and indirect ownership stakes. Indirect ownership is calculated by multiplying the ownership percentages along the chain (e.g., owning 90% of B which owns 80% of A gives 72% indirect ownership in A). If the total ownership reaches or exceeds the applicable beneficial ownership threshold (e.g., 25% as required by most jurisdictions), the individual is considered a UBO; otherwise, not (e.g., D with 82% is a UBO, while C with 18% is not).
source_quotes: most jurisdictions require beneficial ownership to be identified at a threshold of 25% or more
need to identify indirect ownership stakes in addition to direct ownership
owns 10%... directly... 72%... indirectly... then considered a UBO with 82% shareholding
owns 10%... directly... 8% indirectly... is not a UBO

propositions.proposition: Organizations should adopt a risk-based approach to set the appropriate beneficial ownership identification threshold.
source_quotes: Your organization will set the appropriate threshold using a riskbased approach.

propositions.proposition: For high-risk customers, the beneficial ownership threshold may be as low as 10%, and for significantly higher-risk customers, it may go as low as 5% (e.g., high-risk financial institutions with correspondent banking relationships in a high-risk jurisdiction may set their threshold at 5%).
source_quotes: high-risk customers, the beneficial ownership threshold might be as low as 10% and could go as low as 5%
high-risk financial institutions with correspondent banking relationships in a high-risk jurisdiction might set their threshold at 5%

propositions.proposition: When assessing ownership and control, it is important to note that a beneficial owner (BO) may not have control of the company, while an ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) may not directly hold shares but can exert ultimate control.
source_quotes: a BO might appear to have ownership of a company but might not control the company. Conversely, a UBO might not directly hold shares but does exert ultimate control over it.

propositions.proposition: When there is no natural person as UBO, a controller or a notional beneficial owner should be identified and verified (e.g., for a publicly listed company, the president or chief executive officer can be the notional beneficial owner) in order to understand who controls the decision-making in the company.
source_quotes: where there is no natural beneficial owner, a controller or a notional beneficial owner should be identified and verified
publicly listed... a notional beneficial owner could be the president or chief executive officer, or equivalent
